beats.trigger: ## Multi-Agent Systems
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: The filesystem is the meeting room.
beats.got: Agents hand work to each other through files, not through a chat. A bit cute, but at least it's a mechanism.

beats.trigger: [Schedule your personal agent](exercises/personal-agent-homework.md) to read your challenge memory for a week.
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: **Analyze** handoff failures: hidden conflicts, clashing dialects, beige averaging
beats.got: Verb list. 'Beige averaging' I take to mean mush. That is at least a candid failure mode.

beats.trigger: What do you expect will get lost between them?
beats.got: It asks what will go wrong, not what will be great. I notice that.

beats.trigger: The agent writes the exact message first and sends only after approval.
beats.got: Writing a file and sending a message are different risks, and the demo is deliberately small and gated. Sensible, no hype.

beats.trigger: Push back hard when the first answer restates the problem.
beats.got: I get to test it myself on my own material, and I'm told the first answer will be weak. A strategy term I recognise, so useful.

beats.trigger: Skip any retriever you can't run today; two or one still works.
beats.got: Three parallel sessions search wiki, docs and the internet while a fourth merges the results. That is more than I could have done two years ago, and they admit it needs access I may not have.

beats.trigger: You can't yet tell if it is right; that is expected.
beats.got: Helpers with different stances feed one synthesis. They admit I can't yet verify it, which is oddly credible.

beats.trigger: Your team will ask: *when do I split, and how?*
beats.got: Setup for a rule of thumb.

beats.trigger: A mega-agent that does everything drifts in scope, and nobody can tell what it is responsible for.
beats.got: One agent per recurring workflow. Sounds like normal process ownership.

beats.trigger: Inside a workflow, start with don't.
beats.got: The training tells me not to split into more agents by default. A vendor-style course arguing against more of the product is new.

beats.trigger: A backward planner and a reframer in the same voice are one agent pretending to be two.
beats.got: Three tests: different access, dialect or stance. Usable as a checklist.

beats.trigger: Split for a reason, not because "three is more thorough"
beats.got: More agents isn't more rigour. They are warning against the pitch itself.

beats.trigger: The stances bring the variety. The frame brings the choice.
beats.got: Without a framework like Rumelt's kernel, the synthesis just averages. I've seen consultants do the same.

beats.trigger: Could one prompt produce the same quality of output?
beats.got: A simple test to catch overbuilding.

beats.trigger: **Helper agents in one session (the Phase 2 move).**
beats.got: Separate sessions or helpers inside one session. Fine, a bit of jargon.

beats.trigger: Other agents are part of the tool surface: one agent can call a different stance, source zone, or working style.
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: A retriever finds two numbers and the curator keeps one.
beats.got: Concrete failure examples: a number silently dropped, jargon rewritten and its meaning lost. I would check exactly there.

beats.trigger: A whole module showed multi-agent works. Don't apply it to everything.
beats.got: They tell me not to over-apply what they just taught. I appreciate that.

beats.trigger: confident right before a failed handoff.
beats.got: Agents fail and sound sure while doing it. Candid.

beats.trigger: This prompt is long. Make your own variant.
beats.got: Ask the agent whether the bug is in the sources, the processing or the boundary.

beats.trigger: move the risky step from "do" to "propose."
beats.got: A troubleshooting list. Reasonable, standard.

beats.trigger: rewrites the root instructions file in place and reports what changed
beats.got: The agent rewrites its own rules file after a harsh review. OK.

beats.trigger: The audit reads how your agents handed work to each other; it does not check whether the briefing is true.
beats.got: Nothing in the module verifies that the output is true. They say it plainly, and it's what I would have asked.

beats.trigger: Read the agent's summary. Push back where it's wrong
beats.got: Argue with the summary.

beats.trigger: Keep the unease about the synthesized briefing as an open question. Do not fix it today.
beats.got: I'm told to leave my doubt about the result unresolved. Honest, but also unsatisfying.

beats.trigger: Memory is a working artefact, sharpened by what it bumps into.
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: Three stances beat one summarizer.
beats.got: Summary: split only for access, dialect or stance.

beats.trigger: [Agent Trigger List, After Module 3]
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: Agents add non-deterministic behaviour, prompt injection (direct, or inside retrieved text) and emergent capability you can only bound.
beats.got: Agent risk sits on top of normal security. GDPR people will like this part.

beats.trigger: An agent that works across connected systems has access to those systems.
beats.got: Ask what the worst thing is it could do with the access. That is the right question.

beats.trigger: You're close to an agent system that cracks your crux.
beats.got: Keep building. 'Cracks your crux' is a bit much.

take_homes: Default to one agent with one good prompt. Split only for different access, dialect or stance.
The weak points are the handoffs: numbers dropped, jargon rewritten, three views averaged into mush. A framework forces a choice.
Nothing here checks that the synthesized answer is true. I still have to judge that myself.

monday.move: Pick one real strategy question and run the crux prompt on a small slice of our material, then compare it to what my team would say. If it is just a fluent summary, I stop.
monday.when: Tuesday or Wednesday, half an hour between steering groups
monday.stop_condition: The output only restates the problem or shows nothing my team doesn't already know
monday.blocker: Calendar, and whether I can access the wiki and docs from the tool

misconception.why: It didn't sound like the earlier programmes. It argues against using more of itself and admits the output isn't verified. The retrieval run is also something I couldn't have done two years ago. I still wait and see whether it holds up on real work.

one_line: Surprisingly honest: it says 'start with don't' and admits nothing checks whether the answer is true. I'll try one real question before I judge it.
